articles.title: Woman accusing David Walliams of grooming her backs staggered age of consent call

articles.author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey, produced by Nada Smiljanic and Annie La Vespa, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
It is a big week for Andy Burnham as two of his big policy priorities enter the spotlight. On Tuesday, the Milburn review of welfare for under-25s is published, which could ignite old Labour tensions over benefit cuts.
Then, later this week, Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit to discuss a potential new deal. But, as Pippa has signalled, cabinet ministers have told Burnham to put the brake on some of the discussions to ensure the government is not out of step with the public.
Is it too little too late?
You can read Rowena Mason’s article on benefits for under-25s here.
You can watch episodes of Politics Weekly on our YouTube channel here.
Send your questions to Pippa and Kiran on politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Will Burnham put a ‘brake’ on push to rejoin EU? – podcast

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Popular edible golden oyster classed as high-risk invasive species because of negative impact on woodlands
They have been viewed for years as the ideal Christmas gift for the culinary-minded, but experts have now warned that grow-your-own mushroom kits should be blacklisted from a spot under the tree.
An international group of mycologists, including experts from the Royal Horticultural Society, have said many of these kits, which allow people to easily grow mushrooms at home as a delicious addition to stir-fries and other dishes, contain invasive species.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mushroom lovers in UK told to avoid grow kits owing to invasive species risk

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose
articles.description:
Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds

Business live – latest updates

Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis.
The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year

articles.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
articles.description:
Exclusive: Experts say watering down ZEV mandate would slow market and hamper efforts to reduce cost of living
Moves to weaken the UK’s targets on electric vehicles would hurt the car industry as well as consumers, campaigners and experts have said before a key intervention from government advisers expected this week.
The climate change committee (CCC) will write to ministers on Wednesday about the effects of changing the zero emissions vehicle (ZEV) mandate on the cost of living and the UK’s net zero targets.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Weakening UK electric vehicle targets would hurt car industry, ministers told

articles.author: Presented by Kiran Stacey and Jessica Elgot, produced by Saskia Collette, music by Axel Kacoutié; executive producer Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
This week, Kemi Badenoch roasted the prime minister at PMQs with gag after gag. But while the leader of the opposition looks feisty, are some Labour MPs also beginning to wonder if Andy Burnham has the substance to back his policy agenda?
Plus, with the social media ban looking likely to include companies such as Vinted, deputy political editor Jessica Elgot explains the government’s thinking
Read Kiran’s article on jitters about Burnham’s 10-year plan here
Read Jessica’s article on the social media ban here
Send any questions for Pippa and Kiran to politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com
Watch Politics Weekly on our YouTube channel here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Are cracks showing in the Burnham project? – podcast

articles.author: Presented by Nosheen Iqbal with Maeve McClenaghan . Video produced by James Tindale & Eleanor Biggs . Sound design by Eli Block . Motion graphics by Natalie Gegan . Executive produced by Homa Khaleeli, Elizabeth Cassin, Phil Maynard & Rachel Oldroyd
articles.description:
Multiple women allege David Walliams abused his power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were young women, an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found. He denies the allegations.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on this investigation, Walliams writes: 'Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

'I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.'

He adds: 'I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.'
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The allegations against David Walliams | Investigation by the Guardian and ITV News

articles.description:
The former comedian Russell Brand has been sentenced to a total of 10 years and six months for raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women at the height of his career.
Brand was found guilty after a four-week trial at Southwark crown court in which he was described as a ruthless and manipulative sexual predator

Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Judge sentences Russell Brand to more than 10 years in prison – video

articles.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
articles.description:
Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of ‘cacophony’ of noise causing sleep deprivation and depression
When Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home.
“It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester. Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It’s a feeling of being screwed over’: once-quiet village despairs over ‘monster’ warehouse

articles.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
articles.description:
Scheme in Derry aims to sow confidence by getting people with learning and physical disabilities into wrestling
The music thumped, the lights blazed and from the ring the announcer did a countdown. “Who is ready to rumble?” he roared. The bellows and cheers indicated that the crowd at St Columb’s Hall in Derry on Saturday night was more than ready for the Foyle Rumble, and so began a wrestling extravaganza of heroes and villains in leotards, masks and kneepads.
The blend of athleticism and scripted storytelling would have been familiar to fans of WrestleMania, but this Northern Irish version came with a twist: many of the performers have learning or physical disabilities, and the characters they play in the ring do not quite stay in the ring.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘No matter what, he doesn’t quit’: disabled wrestlers draw strength from ring alter egos

articles.author: Chris Osuh, Aamna Mohdin and Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Some relatives of British citizens say they feel left behind, but announcement has brought relief to many care workers
“The only time we’re regarded as human beings is when they need a lot of hands onboard, like during Covid. But after that, we’re tossed away like we’re some rubbish,” Aneisha Williams says.
Williams, 39, was months from qualifying for indefinite leave to remain after 10 years in the UK. But claiming housing benefit could delay her settlement for years under Shabana Mahmood’s “earned settlement” plans.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I feel free now’: Shabana Mahmood’s immigration shake-up provokes mixed emotions

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
With heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movement
The verdict was met with a groan from Tommy Robinson’s supporters, who had sat behind the dock throughout his harassment trial.
It took more than 11 hours of jury deliberations to find the far-right activist guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists, enough time for a band of lieutenants and hangers-on to get their hopes up that he might be acquitted.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership void

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas  
The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns

articles.author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
articles.description:
Reviewers praise relationship between two leads in hotly anticipated release, whose trailer attracted 90m views in 24 hours
Good things clearly come to those who wait. After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here – and, according to critics, it’s a masterpiece.
The trailer for the video game, which returns players to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, attracted more than 90m views in 24 hours when it was released in December 2023. Excitement continued to mount, with two release delays and a steady stream of leaks and speculation keeping the game in the headlines.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Most extraordinary virtual world’: critics hail Grand Theft Auto VI as masterpiece

articles.author: Nick Visser
articles.description:
Players can renovate houses, fix cars, lift weights and follow the story in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Miami-inspired Vice City

Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

Gamers across Australia woke up Thursday morning feeling like Christmas had come early, some bleary-eyed from late-night sessions on the PlayStation, others with grand plans for a weekend foray in Vice City when their day jobs let them loose.
Grand Theft Auto VI, more than a decade in the making, is here. And the reviews, mere hours into release, reflect universal acclaim. The game has already vaulted to the top spot on Metacritic’s list of the best games of all time, sitting above 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time with an unprecedented 99/100 score.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: GTA 6 dazzles gamers in Australia with ‘fully lived-in, breathable world’

articles.author: Sanya Mansoor
articles.description:
Football players say they are ‘traumatized’ after being handcuffed and detained by police while waiting for rides home
Four current and former students at a Maryland high school have filed a lawsuit a year after armed police detained them, prompted by an AI alert that mistook a bag of Doritos for a gun, in an incident that left them “fearing for their lives”.
The plaintiffs sued Omnilert, the company behind the AI gun-detection system, Baltimore county police, the board of education, individual officers and the school principal, alleging unlawful detention and search because of technological and human errors.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Four Maryland high school students sue after AI mistakes Doritos bag for gun

articles.description:
Grand Theft Auto VI has launched, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon. GTA co-creator Dave Jones reflected on the evolution of the popular video game franchise, saying players' preference for playing criminals helped shape the direction of the original game

Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story

We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match

 Continue reading...
articles.title: 'More fun being chased': GTA6 co-creator reflects on franchise's evolution – video

articles.author: Marina Dunbar
articles.description:
Disruption comes at critical moment, with Grand Theft Auto VI one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in history
PlayStation has suffered widespread network problems just hours before the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in recent gaming history.
The disruption emerged Wednesday, causing frustrated players to flood social media with complaints about failed logins and server connection problems downloading games and updates.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: PlayStation suffers widespread network problems hours before release of GTA VI

articles.author: Guardian community team
articles.description:
Grand Theft Auto VI has finally arrived. We’d like to hear your initial thoughts 
It’s been 13 years in the making, and may be the most highly anticipated video game of all time. Grand Theft Auto VI has finally arrived.
The new instalment of the epic crime saga is said to have cost more than $1bn to make and is widely expected to break sales records: some predictions put total sales at 40m copies in its first three months.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

articles.author: Ariana Baio in New York
articles.description:
As Democrats flag AI bank breaches and cyber-attacks in Japan, Jay Clayton says system failures happen

US politics live – latest updates

A bipartisan pair of US senators are calling on Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to identify and fix vulnerabilities in the US’s infrastructure following nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies.
Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce, science, and transportation committee, and Mike Rounds, the Republican chair of the Senate subcommittee on cybersecurity, sent a letter to Clayton on Tuesday, outlining concerns sparked by reports of AI accessing major banks, cyber-attacks in Japan and more.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages

articles.author: Steve May
articles.description:
Not sure which TV is right for you? Whether you want an affordable mini LED or a feature-packed OLED, here’s what our square-eyed expert recommends
• Do you really need to buy a new TV? How to upgrade your setup

If your TV looks like an off-cut from Stonehenge, isn’t quite as smart as your microwave or, heaven forfend, is boring old HD rather than 4K HDR (high dynamic range), it could be time to invest in something more up to date.
But even a cursory look at the latest TVs available will confirm a bewildering array of options, from super-slim models with unfeasibly large screens to high performers that rival the picture quality at your local cinema.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The best TVs in the UK for every home and screen size, tested

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
US secretary of state’s comments come as vulnerability in programming language Java highlighted
There is “zero evidence” that a wave of IT outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access, affected Apple and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or are the work of malign actors, according to the US secretary of state.
Marco Rubio said the US was “not under systemic attack” and a cascade of network problems was “not inter-related”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Zero’ evidence that recent cascade of tech outages are linked, says Rubio

articles.author: Andrew Lawrence
articles.description:
After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement
I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.
Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback

articles.author: Alia Waheed
articles.description:
Tech companies urged to adapt moderation of photos online that can trigger violence against women in some countries
It was just a photo of a smiling girl in jeans and a vest top, the kind of outfit any young woman might wear in any country. But for Maniza*, a teenager from a conservative town in Pakistan who never leaves the house without her hijab, the selfie she took at home put her at very real risk of an “honour” killing.
“My family are really strict and I always wore a hijab. My father didn’t want me to stay in school but my mum pushed him. He said if I got into trouble, he would kill me. It wasn’t just words, he meant it,” she says.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘My family would kill me if they saw it’: the ‘harmless’ images that can be deadly for women in Pakistan

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Research to look at whether ban can make meaningful change in mental health and wellbeing for under-16s
Countries around the world are considering social media bans for children, but whether this would work in practice has been hotly debated. Now researchers are seeking answers through a major scientific study led by Wellcome, which will be the first of its kind.
Ten research projects will explore topics ranging from children’s mental health to their sleep and physical activity, comparing factors before and after the social media ban for children under 16 is introduced in the UK in spring 2027.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: £10m ‘once-in-a-generation’ study to explore effects of children’s social media ban

articles.author: Anna Betts and Blake Montgomery
articles.description:
Google’s Gmail also affected after problems reported in technological infrastructure in the US and worldwide
Thousands reported disruptions to Google’s Gmail and Apple’s iPhone apps, such as Apple Pay and iCloud, on Tuesday, according to Downdetector. Apple confirmed the outages in a statement but said it had resolved them, while Google said it had not seen internal signs of outages.
Apple’s own system status page as of 2.30pmET showed problems with services such as the App Store, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps and AppleCare.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apple outage: iPhone apps suffer disruption days after major Microsoft issues

articles.author: Hilary Osborne
articles.description:
Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history
The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history.
The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?

articles.author: Alan Martin
articles.description:
Tech on its last legs? Refurbished can be the cheaper, greener option. Here’s how to choose well and avoid the pitfalls
• How to make your phone last longer
Even if you do your best to avoid it, it’s hard to escape the noise of retailers offering implausible-seeming Black Friday discounts on desirable technology. What they won’t be so keen to highlight is the huge environmental cost that comes from feeding the capitalist beast year on year, given what an obvious sales vibe-killer it would be.
While the best approach for the planet is to opt out completely and observe the alternative holiday of Buy Nothing Day instead, such an approach can prove self-defeating for your finances in the long term. If you shop smart on Black Friday and avoid the lure of impulse buys, it’s a good time to stock up on the things you need at lower prices than the rest of the year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Don’t buy new tech this Black Friday: expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Agreement secured by Equity union gives actors rights over payment and consent when digital replicas are used
Actors in the UK are to be given more rights over their “digital replicas” as part of a new agreement on AI protections with TV and film producers, secured after a growing on-set backlash.
Under a wide-ranging new deal secured by Equity, the actors’ union, performers will have the rights to be paid when their digital replicas are used and to consent to whether their digital replica is used or not.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Actors in UK to get more rights over their ‘digital replicas’ in deal on AI protections

articles.author: Lauren Almeida
articles.description:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores
Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.
But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Report identifies three factors that led to blackout: a bug, malfunctioning internal connections and server capacity
Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week.
The office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage

articles.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
articles.description:
DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it
Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
articles.description:
Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design
Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.
It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.
Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)
Processor: Apple M6
RAM: 16, 24 or 32GB
Storage: 1, 2 or 4TB SSD
Operating system: macOS 26.4 Tahoe
Camera: 12MP Centre Stage
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones
Dimensions: 221.2 x 312.6 x 15.5mm
Weight: 1.55kg
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation

articles.author: Nils Pratley
articles.description:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability
Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.
It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley

articles.author: Aisha Down
articles.description:
CEO’s affair and resignation has brought company’s murky corporate contracts and supply chains into sharp focus
Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world?
Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
articles.description:
Redesigned flagship laptop has a fantastic display, killer performance and the first touchscreen on a Mac, but comes with a serious price tag
Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac.
The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision
For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large.
He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?

In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.
